Fix temp-file race in parallel script execution and stats lastModified

Temp script filenames used Date.now(), so concurrent executions (the today
resource's three parallel queries, or parallel MCP tool calls) landed in the

task.modificationDate (AppleScript name) instead of the OmniJS property
task.modified. And log a warning when a today-resource query fails instead

Fix #57: verify task persisted before add_omnifocus_task returns success (#85)

add_omnifocus_task could report success for a task that hadn't yet
committed in OmniFocus. OmniFocus commits new objects on its own run
loop, so immediately after `make new task` the record can be briefly
invisible to a fresh `whose id` lookup from another process. An
immediate follow-up edit_item (by the returned id) then finds nothing —
yet add already claimed success. That silent false-success is the worst
failure class: it makes the audit trail lie and every downstream agent
unreliable.

Fix: after the create script returns, confirm the new task is resolvable
by its id in a SEPARATE osascript invocation before reporting success,
retrying on a short backoff (~1.5s worst case, one cheap read when warm).
This waits the commit out — the same effect as the reporter's manual
query-between-calls workaround — and returns an honest failure if the
task truly never lands.

The re-fetch must be a separate process: an in-script re-fetch resolves
the in-memory object even when it isn't yet visible to other processes,
so it cannot distinguish committed from uncommitted (verified
empirically). Living in the primitive, this also hardens batch_add_items,
which feeds a created task's id back as parentTaskId for its children.

Retry logic is extracted as verifyPersistedWithRetries with an injectable
probe/sleep and unit tested for the first-hit, retry-then-hit, and
never-resolves cases.

#80: idle-timeout backstop to reap orphaned stdio servers (#86)

Part of the #80 80/20 (attacks problem A: process accumulation).

When a client is SIGKILL'd, EOF may never reach the server through the
npx → cli.cjs → node wrapper chain (an intermediate wrapper can hold
stdin open), so the existing stdin-EOF + signal handlers don't fire and
the server lingers as an orphan for days — accumulating and contending
for AppleEvents on the single shared OmniFocus.app (the -1712 storms that
wedge multi-agent setups). This adds a last-resort backstop: if no client
traffic arrives within an idle window, exit.

Every JSON-RPC request reaches the server as stdin data (the SDK's stdio
transport also listens on 'data', so our listener is additive and doesn't
disturb it), so each request resets the timer and an actively-used server
never times out — verified with a live smoke test (no-traffic server
idle-exits at the window; a heartbeated server survives and is only
reaped after traffic stops).

Configurable via OMNIFOCUS_MCP_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MINUTES (default 30; 0
disables). Logic lives in src/utils/idleTimeout.ts with unit tests for
env parsing, firing, reset-on-traffic, disable, and disposer.

#80: bound + fast-fail + retry osascript to tame AppleEvent contention (#87)

Second part of the #80 80/20 (attacks problem B: AppleEvent contention).

OmniFocus.app is a single-threaded shared resource; under concurrency it
returns `AppleEvent timed out (-1712)` and, at the default timeout, hangs
each caller ~120s. We can't fix cross-process contention from inside one
server, but a single server can stop making it worse and fail fast
instead of hanging.

Adds a shared osascript runner (runOsascriptFile) that all osascript
invocations now route through, so the bounds actually apply per-process:
- a FIFO Semaphore bounding concurrent osascript children
  (OMNIFOCUS_MCP_MAX_CONCURRENT_OSASCRIPT, default 4),
- a Node-level timeout that kills a stuck osascript instead of hanging
  (OMNIFOCUS_MCP_OSASCRIPT_TIMEOUT_MS, default 60s),
- retry-with-backoff on transient timeouts — but ONLY for idempotent
  reads. A -1712 on a write may have partially applied, so retrying a
  create could duplicate; writes fail fast and honestly (and add already
  has the #57 verify guard).

Routed: executeJXA + executeOmniFocusScript (reads, retry on), and the
add/edit/remove/createTag/addProject primitives (writes, no retry). The
dead exec/promisify imports those primitives no longer need are removed.

Retry policy, retryability detection, and the Semaphore are extracted as
pure, injectable helpers with unit tests (concurrency cap, release-on-
throw, -1712 vs genuine-error classification, retry/no-retry/give-up).

Live smoke test through the routed path: create/edit/query/remove all
succeed and self-clean.

#71: systematic task/project parity test suite for query_omnifocus (#88)

The tasks and projects branches of generateFilterConditions evolve
independently, so a filter added for tasks silently no-ops for projects —
this "tasks work, projects forgotten" drift has shipped at least five
times (#63, #64, #65, the projectId bug in #70, the projectName bug in
#71). The bug half of #71 was fixed in #70; this adds the systematic
suite so the NEXT drift is caught by CI instead of by a user querying
live data.

Approach — a single explicit contract, data-driven:
- FILTER_SPEC declares, for every documented filter, which entities should
  support it (based on the properties each entity actually has).
- The documented filter set is introspected from the live zod schema, so a
  newly added filter fails the suite until its parity is declared.
- generateFilterConditions is asserted to emit a real condition exactly
  when the contract says it should (tasks + projects), and never for
  folders (which support no filters by design).
- Field parity locks the entity-divergent accessors: a project's `id`
  emits the root-task id (#77), tasks/projects use their own status maps.

Surfaced gaps: seven filters that projects SHOULD support (they have the
underlying property) but don't yet — tags, flagged, dueWithin,
deferredUntil, hasNote, dueOn, deferOn — are tracked in an explicit
KNOWN_PROJECT_GAPS set. When one is implemented, the "gaps stay honest"
test fails on purpose, forcing its removal so the contract can't silently
drift back.

54 new tests; suite is pure (no live OmniFocus).

#71: implement the 7 missing project filters, fix 3 silent-empty bugs (#89)

The parity suite added in #88 recorded seven filters that query_omnifocus
documents for projects but only implemented for tasks. This implements them on
the projects branch of generateFilterConditions and empties
KNOWN_PROJECT_GAPS: tags, flagged, dueWithin, deferredUntil, hasNote, dueOn,
deferOn.

Verifying those against the live database turned up three pre-existing bugs of
the same family — filters that ran but silently matched nothing:

1. `Project.added` / `Project.modified` are undefined in OmniJS. Unlike name,
   note, flagged, dueDate, deferDate, tags, completionDate and dropDate, these
   two are NOT forwarded from the root task, so `addedWithin`/`addedOn` on
   projects matched zero rows and the `added`/`modified` fields returned null.
   Confirmed live: 0/43 projects had `.added`, 43/43 had `.task.added`;
   `addedWithin: 100000` returned 0 of 31 projects, now returns 31.

2. `hasNote: false` returned nothing, for tasks as well as projects. An empty
   note makes `item.note && item.note.trim().length > 0` evaluate to "" rather
   than false, so the strict `hasNote !== false` compare rejected every item.
   Live before: 0 of 185 tasks. After: 63 with notes + 122 without = 185.

3. A bare `item.tags.some(...)` would throw inside the filter callback for a
   project with no tags, taking down the whole query rather than returning no
   matches; the projects branch guards with `item.tags || []`.

All seven filters verified against the real database (read-only, no fixtures):
dueOn returned exactly the expected project at each computed day offset, tag
filtering honors OR semantics across a tag array, and flagged/hasNote now
partition the set (1+30=31, 15+16=31).

Tests: 299 passing. The parity contract now expects all 23 documented filters on
their intended entities, plus a new property-routing suite that asserts projects
read `item.task.added` and never `item.added` — emitting code for a filter is
not the same as reading the right property, which is what let these three hide.

Fail loudly when a folder/project path has no usable components (#90)

`generateFolderLookupScript` and `generateProjectLookupScript` both emitted a
bare `set <var> to missing value` — with no error return — for a path that
splits into zero components, e.g. "/" or "//". The caller then falls through to
its default container and reports success for a placement nobody asked for.

That is the silent-success class of bug fixed in #57, and it is about to become
reachable on the creation path: PR #82 wires `generateProjectLookupScript` into
`add_omnifocus_task`, at which point `projectName: "/"` returns
`success: true` with the task created in the INBOX, where main today returns
"Project not found: /". Verified live against both builds before this fix.

Both helpers now emit the caller's error JSON for a component-less path, so the
failure is explicit. Verified live after the fix:

  add_project   folderName: "/"       -> Folder not found: /
  edit_item     newProjectName: "/"   -> Project not found: /

All three call sites (addProject.folderName, editItem.newProjectName,
editItem.newFolderName) already guard against empty/undefined before calling,
so only genuinely degenerate paths change behavior — from silent fallthrough to
an explicit error. The emitted script still sets the variable to `missing value`
first, so the existing assertions continue to hold unchanged.

Fix #91: dates written a month late, and read back a day early (#93)

Two independent bugs, both silent — the call reported success and the
stored/returned date was wrong.

WRITE: month rollover (createDateOutsideTellBlock)

The emitted AppleScript scaffolds off `copy current date`, so the
intermediate carries *today's* day-of-month. Setting the month while that
day is out of range for the target rolls the date forward, and the later
`set day` cannot undo it:

    today = Jul 31, target = Nov 1
      set month to 11  -> Nov 31 invalid -> rolls to Dec 1
      set day to 1     -> already 1, no-op -> stays Dec 1

Any date written on the 29th-31st toward a shorter month landed a month
late, via add_omnifocus_task, add_project and edit_item, for due, defer and
planned alike. Fixed by normalizing the day to 1 before year/month, so every
intermediate is valid in every month. Verified against live AppleScript with
a synthetic Jul-31 base across six targets including leap-Feb.

READ: UTC serialization of local wall-clock dates

Every date field was serialized with `toISOString()`. OmniFocus dates are
local wall-clock times, so in any timezone ahead of UTC local midnight
rendered as the previous calendar day:

    Europe/London (BST), defer = Oct 1 00:00 local
      before: "2026-09-30T23:00:00.000Z"   -> reads as Sep 30
      after:  "2026-10-01T00:00:00+01:00"  -> reads as Oct 1

This was structurally invisible to anyone developing behind UTC, which is
why it survived this long and why no test caught it. The offset-qualified
form fixes the calendar day without losing the instant — it round-trips
through `new Date()` to the same moment.

The reporter diagnosed this half as a write-path bug; it is not. The write
path already normalized date-only input to local midnight (and a live
round-trip confirms it stores correctly). Their suggested fix — UTC getters
for date-only input — would have reintroduced the bug that normalization
exists to prevent, and left the real cause untouched.

Fixed in both halves: the JXA query layer, and the human-readable formatter,
which did `new Date(s).toISOString().slice(0,10)` and so re-broke a correct
input. Fixing only one would have half-landed.

One implementation, no drift

There were four copies of formatDate, all UTC. Rather than patch N places,
src/utils/dateSerialization.ts now owns the single implementation and ships
its own source text into JXA via `formatDate.toString()`, injected as a
prelude by executeOmniFocusScript. Payloads no longer declare their own; a
test asserts they don't, since a redeclaration alongside the prelude's
`const` is a runtime SyntaxError with no compile-time warning.

Tests assert behavior, not emitted text: the injected source is evaluated
and compared against the TypeScript function, so a change that keeps
`toString()` working but breaks the injected copy still fails. That is the
lesson from the three silent-empty query bugs in #71 — code that is emitted
is not code that works.

Verified live: all three date fields round-trip exactly through
add_omnifocus_task, edit_item and query_omnifocus, with correct per-date DST
offsets (-05:00 in Feb, -04:00 in Apr). All four payload-backed tools
(list_tags, list_perspectives, get_perspective_view, dump_database) and
omnifocus://stats confirmed working under the prelude.

Noted while verifying, not fixed here: getChangesSince filters on
task.creationDate/modificationDate, which do not exist in OmniJS (it is
added/modified), so it always returns empty. It is unreachable dead code —
filing separately.

Release v1.10.0

Share one server process across clients via a daemon (#80) (#96)

Every MCP client launched its own OmniFocus server. Two problems followed
from that, and both are the same problem underneath.

Process accumulation: cli.cjs spawned the server as a child with
stdio:'inherit' and then exited, leaving a detached process holding the
client's pipes with no signal handlers and no exit relay. Killing a client
left its server running; the next launch added another.

AppleEvent contention: the osascript concurrency cap in scriptExecution.ts
is module-global, so it bounded each process independently. Ten servers
meant ten budgets of four concurrent osascript children aimed at
single-threaded OmniFocus.app — the direct cause of the -1712 timeouts.

Now `omnifocus-mcp` runs a thin shim that splices stdio onto a Unix socket
served by one shared daemon, starting it if absent. Sessions stay
independent (MCP is stateful, so each connection builds its own McpServer
via the new buildServer.ts factory) but share one process, so the
osascript cap is finally global. cli.cjs imports its entrypoint instead of
spawning it, so signals and exit codes are the process's own.

A Unix socket in a 0700 dir rather than a loopback port: this server can
delete the user's whole database, and file permissions give kernel-enforced
uid access control with no token to mint or leak. It also needs no SDK
bump — StdioServerTransport accepts any (Readable, Writable) pair, and a
net.Socket is both.

Startup is guarded by an atomic-mkdir lock, since a burst of agents
starting at once is this project's normal load rather than an edge case.
Without it, one starter can unlink a socket another just bound and strand
its clients. The daemon reaps itself when idle, reclaims sockets left by
killed daemons, and falls back to a standalone in-process server if
anything about the socket is unusable. OMNIFOCUS_MCP_NO_DAEMON=1 opts out
entirely.

Verified against the live database: three concurrent clients issuing real
read-only tool calls served by one daemon process, and ten simultaneous
cold starts producing exactly one daemon with ten working sessions.

Honor projectId in batch_add_items and report placement (#97) (#98)

batch_add_items accepted `projectId` on task items in the sense that
nothing rejected it — Zod stripped the unknown key, the primitive never
saw it, and every task landed in the inbox while the tool reported
success. Recovering meant noticing by eye and re-homing each task with
edit_item.

Two separate defects, both fixed here:

1. The schemas drifted. `add_omnifocus_task` grew `projectId`;
   `batch_add_items` didn't. Add it to the item schema, to
   BatchAddItemsParams, and to the taskParams forwarding, with
   `add_omnifocus_task`'s wording so the guidance stays consistent.

2. The batch result reported no placement at all, so even with the
   argument plumbed through, a future silent fallthrough would look
   exactly like success. `addOmniFocusTask` already returns `placement`;
   batchAddItems discarded it. Carry it through and render it per item,
   warning when a requested project or parent wasn't honored, and hoist
   the count into the summary line for callers that read only the first
   line.

Also targets a batch-created project by its id rather than its name when
resolving parentTempId. Both are the AppleScript namespace, and a batch
creating a project whose name already exists elsewhere would otherwise
attach children to the wrong one.

Verified live against OmniFocus with TEST:-prefixed fixtures: explicit
projectId now lands in the project, a bogus projectId fails loudly
instead of falling through to the inbox, and an unplaced task still
reports plain "inbox" with no warning.

Fix folder path and parentFolderID in query_omnifocus (#95) (#101)

`path` and `parentFolderID` both read `container`, which exists on no OmniJS
class. Verified live against OmniFocus 4.x: 0/17 folders, 0/970 tasks and 0/81
projects have `.container`; 9/17 folders have a `.parent`.

So `path` always took the else branch and returned the bare folder name, and
`parentFolderID` — which had no branch of its own — fell through to the generic
default `item.parentFolderID`, not an OmniJS property either, and returned null.
Neither errored. query_omnifocus simply described a flat database, and anything
reasoning about folder nesting silently recorded the wrong hierarchy.

Changes:
- Walk `parent` to build the full path instead of reading one level. Depth > 1 is
  real (`PhD/Dissertation/Project 3`), and `container.name + "/" + item.name`
  could not have produced it even if `container` existed. `parent` is null at the
  top level, which terminates the walk.
- Implement `parentFolderID` as `item.parent ? item.parent.id.primaryKey : null`,
  matching omnifocusDump.js — dump_database has read folder parentage correctly
  all along, so the two tools disagreed.
- Fix the default folder projection as well as the explicit-fields path; most
  callers never pass `fields`.
- Render `parentFolderID` and subfolder count in formatFolders, which previously
  dropped both. Suppress `path` when it merely echoes the name: "📍 Health" beside
  "F: Health" reads as a located folder rather than an unlocated one, which is
  part of how this stayed invisible.
- Leave `path` on tasks/projects as the bare name. They have a parent chain, but
  `path` is documented as a folder field and walking theirs would quietly define
  new semantics.

Adds property-routing assertions mirroring the ones from #89: they assert the
property actually read, since a presence-only test passes on null — which is
exactly how this hid.

Live after the fix: 9/17 folders nested, max depth 3.

Version the daemon socket filename (#99) (#102)

The socket path contained no version identity and the shim treated "something
is listening" as success, so after an upgrade newly launched clients kept being
served by the old daemon — silently, with a new version number installed.

It did not self-heal either. The idle reaper only arms at zero connections, so a
stale daemon's lifetime is the max over all its clients rather than the idle
window. MCP clients here are long-lived — an editor session can hold one open
for days — so on a busy machine the connection count may never reach zero and
the old daemon can outlive the upgrade indefinitely, with each new arrival
extending it. Because the daemon is shared, one stale process serves every
client on the box.

Fix: SOCKET_FILENAME is now `daemon-<version>.sock`, making it structurally
impossible for a new shim to reach an old daemon rather than merely unlikely.
The cost is one orphaned daemon per upgrade, reaped by the existing idle timer
once its last client leaves — a bounded, self-clearing resource cost in exchange
for a silent correctness bug.

- Extract SERVER_VERSION into src/version.ts. The shim needs the version but must
  not import buildServer to get it; the point of the shim is that it starts
  without building an McpServer or touching the OmniFocus bridge.
- Add VERSION_SLUG, which collapses anything outside [A-Za-z0-9._-]. Semver
  permits `+` build metadata, and a `/` from a fork would silently redirect the
  socket into a directory that does not exist.
- The lock dir is derived from the socket path, so it is versioned for free — a
  new daemon never waits on a lock the old one holds.
- resolveSocketDir already measures join(dir, SOCKET_FILENAME) against
  MAX_SOCKET_PATH_LENGTH, so the longer name is accounted for before bind().

Verified by simulating an upgrade end to end: with a 1.11.0 daemon running, a
1.12.0 client reported 1.12.0 on its own socket, and both daemons coexisted
(daemon-1.11.0.sock, daemon-1.12.0.sock). Before this change the 1.12.0 client
would have reported 1.11.0.

Release v1.12.0

Fix JSON corruption from quotes in names in write results (#103) (#108)

Write primitives build their result JSON by splicing strings into AppleScript
source. escapeAppleScriptString kept the *source* well-formed, but at runtime
the escaped quote re-materialized raw inside the JSON payload, so JSON.parse
failed on our side and the tool reported an error for a write that had
succeeded — a duplicate-retry hazard.

Two defenses, by when the value is known:

Stop retries from deepening OmniFocus AppleEvent wedges (#121) (#122)

The retry predicate treated our own SIGTERM kill as transient contention, so a
read would replay its full query up to three times, 500ms/1500ms apart, into an
app that had already failed to answer for 60s. A process sample of a wedged
OmniFocus shows the cost: eight blocked receiveFrom-<pid> AppleEvent dispatch
queues, one per osascript we killed — four from a concurrency burst, four from
retries. Nothing on our side can release them; only killing the app can. So
every retry inflicted a permanent wound.

  contended -> retry is fine) from a client-kill (app never answered -> do not
  retry). Our 60s timeout fires before AppleEvent's ~120s, so the kill was the
  dominant case on the path least safe for it.
- A process-wide circuit breaker fails fast with AppUnresponsiveError while the
  app is known dead, instead of letting each queued query burn a full timeout
  and leave another orphaned queue. Verified to block in 0ms.
- After a cooldown, one cheap liveness probe (5s, bypasses the semaphore so
  wedged queries cannot starve it) decides whether to resume — at most one
  transaction risked per cooldown rather than a full query.
- Backoffs lengthened 500/1500ms -> 2s/6s; sub-second gaps gave a contended app
  no room to drain.

unsafe to use alone as a retry gate.

Ping the client on idle instead of exiting (#126) (#127)

* Add a client liveness probe for the idle backstop

The idle backstop from #80 protects against a real case — a SIGKILL'd
client whose wrapper chain holds stdin open never sends EOF, and the
stranded process pins a daemon session forever. But silence is not proof
of death, and the backstop resolved that ambiguity by exiting. For a
client that treats a stdio server exit as terminal (#123), a long-lived
session that simply went half an hour without an OmniFocus call loses its
tools for good (#126).

Asking is cheap: server -> client `ping` is part of the protocol and every
conformant client answers it. This is that mechanism as a standalone unit,
so it can be tested without a live daemon: write the ping, watch the
client -> daemon stream for the answer, report alive or dead.

Two details carry the risk. The id is a prefixed string, because this
request is injected into a stream the shim otherwise only forwards and
must not collide with the client's or the daemon's own numbering. And the
answer has to be removed before it reaches the daemon, which never sent
the ping and has no business receiving a response to a request it did not
make. The SDK we pin discards an unknown-id response quietly today, but
only because the callback it routes to is left unassigned — an unwired
hook rather than a contract, and not something a shim should stake a
session on.

So the filter drops exactly that one line and its newline, forwards every
other byte verbatim on line boundaries, and disengages as soon as the
probe resolves. Any other client traffic during the window counts as
liveness too. What goes in comes out unchanged, provided the caller
decodes its input statefully — the tests pin that, including a multi-byte
character split across chunk boundaries.

Claude Code sessions lost OmniFocus tools on a recurring cycle: the shim
